Afraid? I mean... I guess "afraid" doesn't really even begin to cover it. It's more like this absolute, overwhelming panic. Just the idea of the number on the scale going up, even by one single pound, it completely paralyzes me. I can't even describe the anxiety it gives me.

It honestly feels like everyone around me will look at me and instantly be able to see that I’ve completely lost my discipline.

So the thought of just letting that go, of eating something with butter and letting my body get out of control... people notice that stuff. They notice when you let yourself go and stop trying. They'll just know I failed. So yeah, I guess I am terrified of it, because I just can't be that person who loses her grip on things.

I mean... I don't really know how to answer that, because what even is a "normal" weight, you know? Like, normal for who? Normal for the health center's little chart? Because if I were at the weight they think I should be at... I just... I don't know if I'd use the word "fat," exactly, but I know I would feel completely awful. I would feel heavy, and slow, and just... wrong. 

Like, right now, I feel like I'm exactly where I need to be to get everything done. I can feel my bones, and I know exactly where my body is in space, and it just feels right. It feels tight and controlled. If I were at that heavier weight they want me at, I just know my clothes wouldn't fit the same, and I'd feel it every time I moved, every time I sat down in a lecture hall or walked across campus. I'd feel all this extra... just, excess. And I can't stand the thought of having excess anything right now. I don't have excess time, I don't have excess energy to waste, so why should I have excess on my body? 

So, I don't know if I'd look in the mirror and literally see the word "fat" flashing in neon lights, but I know I would look at myself and see someone who gave up. I would see someone who compromised and let herself get soft. And I just... I can't do that. I can't be that person. I don't even like thinking about what I would look like if I gained that weight, because it just makes my skin crawl. It's not even just about the aesthetic, it's about the feeling of it. Does that make sense? I just... I don't think I could handle looking at myself if I let my body get to that so-called "normal" place.

Excessive? Um... no. No, definitely not. I mean, I don't even really know how someone would do that, to be honest. The idea of just sitting down and eating a huge amount of food all at once... it just doesn't compute for me. Like, I have my routine, you know? Like, for example, yesterday, I had my coffee before my 8 AM seminar, and then I had this tiny little container of blueberries that I portioned out the night before—exactly a quarter cup—and I ate that around 11:30 when I had a break between classes, and then... well, you get the idea. It's very structured. If I were to just suddenly eat a whole bunch of food, it would throw off the entire schedule, the entire balance of my day. And I can't afford to be thrown off balance right now. 

I see people in the dining hall sometimes, and they'll just have these massive plates piled high with pasta, and pizza, and then they go back for dessert, and they eat it all in like, twenty minutes. And I just sit there and watch them, and I literally cannot fathom how they do it. Doesn't it hurt? Doesn't it make them feel completely exhausted and sick? If I ate even a fraction of that, I wouldn't be able to study for the rest of the night. I'd just be sitting in the library feeling my stomach stretch and digest, and that's so distracting. 

So no, I don't ever do that. I don't think I've eaten an excessive amount of food in... I don't even know how long. Years, maybe? I just stick to what I know I need to keep going. It's precise. It has to be precise. If I just started eating excessively, everything else would just fall apart.

My period? Um... no, not really. I mean, I guess it depends on what you mean by "recently." Because I haven't had one in... wow, I don't even know. A really long time. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Lost control? No... no, definitely not. Honestly, the idea of losing control while eating is just... it's terrifying to even think about. I am always, always in control. That's kind of the whole point, isn't it? Like, if I lose control of that, what else falls apart? 

I was just talking to my roommate about something like this the other day—well, not this exactly, but she was complaining about how she stress-eats when we have midterms. She was telling me how she'll just open a bag of chips while reading her sociology textbook, and suddenly the whole bag is gone, and she doesn't even remember eating it. She called it "zoning out." And I just sat there looking at her like she had two heads. Because I cannot even comprehend how your brain allows you to do that. How do you just... zone out? How do you not know exactly what is going into your body at every given second? 

For me, eating is... it requires my full, absolute attention. It's a conscious, deliberate decision every single time. I know exactly what I'm doing. I know the exact weight of the apple slices I put in my little Tupperware container, I know exactly what time I'm allowed to open it, and I know exactly how I'm going to eat it. It's like... it's like a math equation. You don't just lose control in the middle of solving a calculus problem, you know? You have to follow the steps. You have to be precise. If I were to just snap and start eating without thinking, without measuring and planning, I would feel this overwhelming, suffocating panic. 

My whole life right now is about keeping everything tightly managed. The mentoring workshop applications, the papers, the reading assignments... I have a color-coded planner that dictates my entire week down to the fifteen-minute mark. Eating is just another part of that grid. It has to be. So, losing control? No. I've never felt that way. I feel the exact opposite. I feel so hyper-aware and so dialed in that sometimes it's exhausting, but it's a good kind of exhausting. It's the kind of exhausting that means I'm doing it right. I'm steering the ship. I would never just let go of the wheel like that, especially not with food. It just... it goes against every single fiber of how I operate.

I mean... I think it’s both? Or, like, they are so intertwined at this point that I can’t really separate them anymore. Because how I look completely dictates how I feel about myself as a person. I'd feel lazy, like I let my guard down, like everything I've been working so hard for is just a joke. So the fear of gaining weight... it's the fear of losing that identity. My shape is basically the physical evidence of my work ethic. Does that make sense? The physical smallness is what allows me to feel mentally sharp and capable. I can't be a serious student, or a serious person, if I take up too much space. The space I take up has to be minimal so I can focus all my energy on my actual goals. I don't go hide in a bathroom stall or sneak off to my dorm room. I just eat it. Sometimes people will make comments, like, \"Oh, is that all you're having?\" or \"You eat like a bird,\" but it doesn't bother me. I just tell them that eating a heavy meal makes me sluggish and I need to stay sharp for whatever we're working on. Which is completely true! I don't see why I should have to conceal my discipline. \n\nI actually think eating in secret would feel... I don't know, it would feel really chaotic to me. It goes back to that whole idea of losing control that you asked about earlier. Like my roommate and her stress-eating. She’ll sometimes hide her candy wrappers in the bottom of the trash can so I won't see them, which I always notice anyway, but... I just can't relate to that mindset at all. \n\nEverything I do is so calculated and intentional. I have my plan written out in my notebook, right next to my assignment deadlines and my workshop meetings. I leave it open on my desk. I don't care who sees it. It's just data. It's just a record of my efficiency. If I were to start hiding when I eat or what I eat, it would feel like I was undermining my own system. It would feel sneaky and messy, and I really, really don't do messy. Everything in my life has to be completely transparent and accounted for, so... no. I definitely don't eat in secret. I can't even imagine just putting food into my mouth without thinking about it or registering every single detail of what it is and how it fits into my daily allotment. \n\nPlus, if I eat too fast, or if I eat even a fraction more than what I had scheduled in my planner, I get this horrible, heavy feeling. I literally watch the clock on my phone or the one on the library wall to pace myself. \n\nI think if I were to eat quickly, it would just feel like this chaotic blur. How does your body even process that? It honestly gives me anxiety just watching people eat fast like that. It’s so mindless. \n\nSo, no, I never have episodes where I eat faster than usual. Well, I mean, I don't really see it as this huge, dramatic drop like people are making it out to be. The entire reason I'm even sitting here talking to you right now is actually because of the Student Health center. I had to go in for what I thought was just going to be a basic, five-minute physical clearance. I volunteer for these youth workshops—it's this program where we mentor high school kids, which is super important for my resume and I've spent weeks preparing my materials for it—and you have to get a medical sign-off to participate. I thought I’d just walk in, get the signature, and go right back to my study carrel. 

But they weighed me, and suddenly it was this massive ordeal. They literally refused to sign the form. Student health sent me here because they say my weight is too low to clear me for the youth workshops. I literally watch the clock on my phone or the one on the library wall to pace myself. \n\nI think if I were to eat quickly, it would just feel like this chaotic blur. It would feel like I wasn't present, and I need to be completely present and aware of every single thing I'm consuming. My roommate, for example, she'll just inhale a bagel on her way out the door to her chem lab, literally walking down the hallway chewing and talking at the same time, and I just watch her and think... how can you even register what you just did? How does your body even process that? It honestly gives me anxiety just watching people eat fast like that. It’s so mindless. \n\nSo, no, I never have episodes where I eat faster than usual. My \"usual\" is incredibly, incredibly slow. I'll sit in the dining hall with my notebook open, and I'll read an entire chapter for my seminar between bites. Because if I speed up, I lose the structure. And if I lose the structure, I lose my focus, and I start to feel out of control. So speed is just... it's completely out of the question for me. I have to draw it out as long as physically possible.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever made yourself vomit after eating?\n\nPatient: Vomit? Oh, no. God, no. Just the thought of that is... no. That completely goes back to the whole \"messy\" thing I was talking about earlier. Making yourself throw up is so incredibly chaotic and, honestly, it just seems so desperate. Like, if someone is doing that, it means they’ve already messed up their plan, right? They ate something they weren't supposed to, or they lost control and ate too much, and now they're panicking and trying to physically undo it. But I never, ever put myself in a position where I need to undo anything, because my intake is already perfectly calculated beforehand. There are no mistakes to erase. \n\nAnd physically, it just sounds horrific. It’s a total loss of bodily control. My body is a machine, and I run it on very specific, very clean fuel. The idea of violently reversing that process... it just doesn't fit into my system at all. Plus, it's so inefficient. I've read about what it does to your body—it ruins your teeth, it messes up your throat, it makes your face all swollen and puffy. I can't have my throat hurting when I have to participate in my seminars. I have a huge presentation in my political science class next Tuesday, and my voice needs to be perfectly clear. I have to be sharp. I can't be dealing with the physical aftermath of something so destructive. \n\nIt just seems like a frantic reaction, and I am never frantic. I am always completely in control of what goes in, so I never, ever have to worry about forcing it out. It just wouldn't make any logical sense for me to do something like that. So, no, absolutely not. Never.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever used laxatives or diuretics to help control your weight?\n\nPatient: Laxatives? Diuretics? No, definitely not. That... that falls into the exact same category as throwing up, in my mind. It's just another way of trying to cheat the system after you've already failed, you know? Like, if you have to resort to taking pills to force your body to flush things out, it means you didn't have the discipline to restrict what went in in the first place. And discipline is literally the foundation of my entire routine. \n\nPlus, taking a pill to make yourself go to the bathroom... it just sounds so unpredictable. And I cannot handle unpredictability. What if it hits you when you're in the middle of a lecture? Or when I'm studying in the quiet section of the library? I practically live on the fourth floor of the library right now because I have two huge papers due before midterms, and I have this one specific carrel by the window that I always use. I can't be running back and forth to the bathroom, worrying about when a laxative is going to kick in. That would completely ruin my focus. I need to be able to sit there for four, five, six hours at a time without any interruptions. \n\nAnd diuretics... that's just messing with your water weight, right? It's fake. It's a temporary fix. It doesn't actually mean you've achieved anything real. My whole process is about real, measurable results based on pure control and restriction. I don't need artificial shortcuts. If I feel like I'm retaining water, or if I feel \"heavy\"—which, like I said, only happens if I somehow miscalculate, which is incredibly rare—I just adjust my water intake very carefully and maybe increase my walking time between classes. I don't take chemicals to force my body to do something. \n\nMy body is supposed to be clean. It's supposed to be empty and efficient. Putting a bunch of harsh pharmacy pills into my system just feels toxic. It feels dirty. It would completely disrupt the purity of what I'm doing. So, no, I would never use anything like that. I don't need them because I don't make the kind of mistakes that would require them. I just stick to my plan. It's safer that way. It's the only way that makes sense.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost a significant amount of weight in a short period of time?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean, I don't really see it as this huge, dramatic drop like people are making it out to be. The entire reason I'm even sitting here talking to you right now is actually because of the Student Health center. I had to go in for what I thought was just going to be a basic, five-minute physical clearance. I volunteer for these youth workshops—it's this program where we mentor high school kids, which is super important for my resume and I've spent weeks preparing my materials for it—and you have to get a medical sign-off to participate. I thought I’d just walk in, get the signature, and go right back to my study carrel. \n\nBut they weighed me, and suddenly it was this massive ordeal. They literally refused to sign the form. Student health sent me here because they say my weight is too low to clear me for the youth workshops. It just feels like what happens when I’m focused and busy. Like I was telling you, I’m taking advanced seminars, I have those massive papers due, I'm prepping for these workshops... If those areas aren't perfectly tight and small, the whole image just falls apart.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your weight or body shape is abnormal even when others tell you it is not?\n\nPatient: I mean, I hear what they’re saying. It doesn't actually mean you've achieved anything real. My whole process is about real, measurable results based on pure control and restriction. I don't need artificial shortcuts. If I feel like I'm retaining water, or if I feel \"heavy\"—which, like I said, only happens if I somehow miscalculate, which is incredibly rare—I just adjust my water intake very carefully and maybe increase my walking time between classes. I don't take chemicals to force my body to do something. \n\nMy body is supposed to be clean. It's supposed to be empty and efficient. Putting a bunch of harsh pharmacy pills into my system just feels toxic. It feels dirty. It would completely disrupt the purity of what I'm doing. So, no, I would never use anything like that. I don't need them because I don't make the kind of mistakes that would require them. I just stick to my plan. It's safer that way. It's the only way that makes sense.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost a significant amount of weight in a short period of time?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean, I don't really see it as this huge, dramatic drop like people are making it out to be. The entire reason I'm even sitting here talking to you right now is actually because of the Student Health center. I had to go in for what I thought was just going to be a basic, five-minute physical clearance. I volunteer for these youth workshops—it's this program where we mentor high school kids, which is super important for my resume and I've spent weeks preparing my materials for it—and you have to get a medical sign-off to participate. I thought I’d just walk in, get the signature, and go right back to my study carrel. \n\nBut they weighed me, and suddenly it was this massive ordeal. They literally refused to sign the form. Student health sent me here because they say my weight is too low to clear me for the youth workshops. Which is just... it's so incredibly frustrating because it completely disrupts my schedule and my plans. And yeah, they showed me my chart and made this big point about how the number has kept dropping, especially recently, but they were acting like it's some sort of emergency. \n\nTo me, honestly? It just feels like what happens when I’m focused and busy. Like I was telling you, I’m taking advanced seminars, I have those massive papers due, I'm prepping for these workshops... I'm just operating at a very high level right now. When you have that much on your plate, and you're that dialed into your routine, you don't have time for excess. It's just a natural byproduct of being disciplined and staying focused on my goals. So, yes, I guess the number has gone down, and it's kept dropping, but it's not a problem. It's just efficiency. I don't understand why they can't just see that and sign my form so I can get back to my students.\n\nDoctor: Are there specific areas of your body where you're particularly concerned about gaining weight?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean, it's not so much about gaining weight in one specific area, it's more about... it's about the overall shape and how it translates to, I guess, my presence? Like, okay, so last month, my art history seminar had this end-of-term showcase. It was a huge deal, all the faculty were there, and we had to present our final projects. I had been working on mine for literally weeks, pulling all-nighters, making sure every single detail was perfect. And of course, people were taking pictures the whole time. \n\nWhen I got the link to the photo gallery afterwards, I didn't even look at the artwork first. It's about whether I'm meeting my own standards, whether I'm maintaining the control I need to get through everything I have to do. If I meet those standards, then it's right. So, yeah, it's acceptable to me, but only when it meets that specific criteria I have for myself, because that's what tells me I'm actually doing things right, regardless of whatever everyone else is saying."
